Field surveys of the Rock goby (Gobius paganellus) in intertidal pools along the Atlantic coast of Europe have established that individuals typically attain a maximum total length of 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters], a size that is rarely exceeded even in the most productive habitats. Newly hatched larvae emerge from demersal eggs with a wet weight of only 0.0011 grams [Wwb = 0.0011 grams], reflecting the modest yolk reserves provisioned within the parentally guarded clutch. This extremely low birth mass, comparable to that of other small-bodied gobiids, necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding shortly after the chorion ruptures. The embryonic development rate and the timing of the hatching event are strongly modulated by ambient temperature, with faster development observed in warmer waters typical of the species' southern range. The shift from lecithotrophic to exotrophic nutrition marks a critical mortality bottleneck, as the tiny prolarvae must locate sufficient microzooplankton prey to sustain growth beyond the yolk-sac stage.

As juveniles grow and begin to occupy permanent territories beneath stones and within crevices, their body length increases steadily until the onset of gonadal differentiation. Puberty in the Rock goby is attained when individuals reach a total length of approximately 6 centimeters [Lp = approximately 6 centimeters], a size that corresponds to a wet weight of about 2.4 grams [Wwp = about 2.4 grams] based on local length-weight relationships. This morphological threshold is reached after a developmental period of 912 days since birth [tp = 912 days since birth] when the fish are reared under stable thermal conditions of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. The delay to maturity is considerably longer than in many temperate gobies, likely reflecting the energetic demands of reaching a sufficiently large body size to defend a nesting site and produce a viable first clutch. Before this point, the immature fish allocate most of their ingested energy toward somatic growth and the accumulation of fat reserves necessary for overwintering.

Reproductive activity in the Rock goby is tightly linked to seasonal temperature cycles, and under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the maximum annual reproductive output has been quantified. At this temperature, females deposit approximately 8978 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 8978 eggs per year], a figure that combines moderate clutch sizes with a protracted spawning season during which multiple broods are produced. The frequency of spawning events is remarkably high for a fish of this body size, reflecting the iteroparous strategy that allows females to capitalize on extended periods of favorable food availability. Each breeding event begins with the male excavating a sheltered nest cavity and attracting a gravid female, who then attaches the adhesive, yolk-laden eggs to the ceiling of the chamber. The male subsequently guards the developing embryos fanning them with his pectoral fins until the eyed eggs hatch into free-swimming prolarvae.

The maximum adult body mass recorded for the Rock goby reaches 24.4 grams [Wwi = 24.4 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions applied to the largest individuals observed in field samples. This ultimate wet weight is attained only after several growing seasons, as the fish approach their asymptotic size near the upper boundary of the species' known length range. At this stage, the body condition of mature individuals becomes a strong predictor of overwinter survival and subsequent fecundity in the following breeding season. Longevity in wild populations, under the standard thermal regime of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], has been estimated at 10 years [am = 10 years], a considerable lifespan for a small intertidal fish that faces high predation pressure from birds and larger piscivores. This extended lifespan allows for multiple reproductive opportunities across successive years, buffering the population against occasional recruitment failures caused by harsh winters or storm events that scour the intertidal zone.

Comparative studies with congeneric species highlight the ecological uniqueness of the Rock goby's life-history strategy. While many small-bodied gobies exhibit a semelparous death following a single intense spawning season, Gobius paganellus is distinctly iteroparous, with senescent adult death typically occurring only after several breeding cycles have been completed. The demographic data collected at 17 °C [T = 17 °C] suggest that the natural mortality rate accelerates after approximately a decade [am = approximately a decade], when individuals begin to show signs of physiological deterioration and reduced competitive ability for nesting sites. At the population level, this longevity, combined with the moderate body size at puberty of 6 centimeters [Lp = 6 centimeters], ensures that a substantial fraction of the adult population remains reproductively viable even in years when juvenile recruitment is low. Field recapture data further indicate that post-reproductive mortality is not abrupt; instead, a gradual decline in body condition and feeding efficiency precedes the eventual death of the organism.
